thread.title: UPDATE: Apple to buy back whopping $100 billion in shares, hike dividend

author: morningstar.com
title: UPDATE: Apple to buy back whopping $100 billion in shares, hike dividend
text:
By Emily Bary
Apple also says it will speed up previous plans to repurchase $210 billion in shares
Though not as sexy as iPhone sales, Apple Inc.'s capital-allocation update may have been the biggest bit of news to come out of Apple's earnings report.
Apple (AAPL) said Tuesday afternoon it would buy back $100 billion in shares and raise its quarterly dividend 16%, to 73 cents a share from 63 cents a share.
Read: Apple earnings to focus on iPhone sales, billions for investors: Live blog (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/apple-earnings-to-focus-on-iphone-sales-billions-for-investors-live-blog-2018-05-01)
The buyback is one of the largest in U.S. corporate history, though the company did not give a specific timeline as to when it will be carried out. "The amount of buybacks we're announcing is so large that it's going to take us some time to execute," Chief Financial Officer Luca Maestri told the Wall Street Journal (https://www.wsj.com/articles/apple-raises-bar-with-stock-buyback-plans-1525209324?mod=mktw). "Our plan is to do it at a fast pace."
Apple also said it would speed up its plan to repurchase $210 billion in shares, with completion sought by the end of June rather than March 2019, as previously planned.
Last quarter, Apple said that it plans to become net-cash neutral "over time." The tech giant has a demonstrated preference (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/apple-analyst-lays-out-path-to-zero-net-cash-deems-transformational-ma-unlikely-2018-02-14)for returning most of its cash to shareholders, and has some $160 billion to spend if it hopes to achieve this goal.
Don't miss: What to look for in Apple's earnings report (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/apple-earnings-iphone-expectations-are-down-but-anxiety-is-still-high-2018-04-27)
Apple boosted its capital-return program by $50 billion (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/the-annual-apple-cash-bonanza-is-here-will-300-billion-be-enough-2017-05-02) a year ago, bringing the cumulative total to about $300 billion through March 2019. Though it was well-established that the program will increase this year, analysts were split on the specifics before the announcement.
One of the most optimistic on the dividend front was Wells Fargo analyst Aaron Rakers, who has a market perform rating on the stock and a $195 target.
"Apple has increased its cumulative capital return program by $30 billion to $50 billion in each of the past five years," he wrote. "We now consider whether Apple could outline a >30% dividend increase (versus +11% average over the past four years, though maintaining a $11 billion to $12 billion [a year] payout) and an incremental $100 billion-plus share [repurchase] program."
See also: Here's why dollar traders are watching Apple's earnings (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/heres-why-dollar-traders-are-watching-apples-earnings-2018-05-01)
Bernstein analyst Toni Sacconaghi sees the company raising its total shareholder-return allocation by $180 billion over the next 2 1/2 years, through incremental buybacks of $50 billion annually as well as a 15% to 20% boost to the dividend. Such efforts could lift fiscal 2018 earnings per share by 12 cents, he argued, and fiscal 2019 earnings per share by 79 cents. Sacconaghi has a market perform rating and a $170 price target on the stock.
See also:Three ways Apple could spend $163 billion besides a big acquisition (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/three-ways-apple-could-spend-163-billion-besides-a-big-acquisition-2018-03-16)
The prospect of increased capital returns has likely given shares a lift since the December-quarter earnings release, so there's debate as to how much the actual news can jolt shares further, especially amid perceived weakness in iPhone demand (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/apple-earnings-iphone-expectations-are-down-but-anxiety-is-still-high-2018-04-27).
Daryanani is relatively upbeat, writing that Apple "has the potential to positively surprise" with both its shareholder-return program as well as increases in the iPhone's average selling price.
Bernstein's Sacconaghi, however, thinks we're ultimately still living in an iPhone world.
"While Apple's expected large capital return program could mitigate the impact to earnings from weak iPhone, we think that on net, fiscal 2018 and fiscal 2019 earnings are more likely to go down than up," he wrote. "Moreover, we believe that the investor narrative post-earnings will likely be dominated by the question of whether the iPhone business can grow over time."
See also: Apple CEO Tim Cook has some harsh words for Facebook (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/apple-ceo-tim-cook-has-some-harsh-words-for-facebook-2018-03-28)
Though Apple CFO Maestri was vague when saying that Apple wants to become net-cash neutral "over time," investors should expect clarity on the time frame with the coming update. It's also worth noting that while Apple tends to return most of its cash to shareholders, it will likely keep some aside for smaller deals, original content (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/three-ways-apple-could-spend-163-billion-besides-a-big-acquisition-2018-03-16) and its plans to invest in both data centers (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/apple-didnt-say-it-was-hiring-20000-new-workers-nor-bringing-back-its-overseas-cash-2018-01-17) and other technological areas.
Apple shares are up 14% in the past 12 months, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average , of which Apple is a component, has gained 16% and the S&P 500 index has increased 12%.
-Emily Bary;
